docs.title: Humble is primary; Foxy is kept alive through backports, not dual-distro code
docs.text:
All Pilsbot repositories get a humble and a foxy branch. Repositories that used foxy-devel rename it to foxy. Repositories that used main/master branch both lines from there, and later move main/master forward to humble. New work lands on the Humble line. Substantial improvements that do not depend on the distro are cherry-picked to the Foxy line: ROS-free cores, bug fixes, the frame re-root, and the robot profile. The ros2_control adapters and launch-API changes stay Humble-only.

We rejected making every package build on both distros (#if on ros2_control versions). The hardware and controller APIs changed completely between Foxy and Humble, so this would roughly double the work in the code that is riskiest to change. Backporting stays cheap because the logic worth backporting is deliberately kept free of ROS.

Only our own code is ported. Third-party packages are consumed as their upstream or the Humble binaries provide them.

docs.title: The robot reference point moves from the front axle to the rear axle centre
docs.text:
base_link used to be the front axle. The chassis and the OAK hung off the steering joint, so the camera's pose relative to base_link changed with every steering angle. This breaks the assumptions of visual SLAM and of the Ackermann planners. base_link now sits at the rear axle centre, with base_footprint on the ground below it. The odometry frame is renamed from odom_raw to odom.

The odometry estimator is deliberately left unchanged. Its front-axle pose is converted to the rear axle centre by a pure frame transform that uses the measured steering angle and the wheelbase. That transform is the same ROS-free function the legacy-log converter uses, so live data and translated Kohlfahrt logs agree by construction. Replacing the estimator with a bicycle model is a separate, later decision.

The controller publishes the result as odom → base_footprint, and the URDF root is base_footprint with base_link one wheel radius above it. The published twist is the same pure transform applied to velocities: the chassis yaws at the front-axle yaw rate plus the steering rate, which is differenced from consecutive steering measurements. It is deliberately not the no-slip bicycle constraint. Any lateral velocity it reports at the rear axle is the estimator's inconsistency made visible, not hidden.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Kohlfahrt logs recorded since Feb 2023 contain no /tf. A missing comma in log_kohl.launch.py merged it into /stereo/camera_info/tf. The converter rebuilds TF from the recorded /robot_description, /joint_states, and /odom, and writes MCAP.
  • The wheelbase must be measured on the robot. The old values disagree: 0.67 in the controller config and about 0.68 in the URDF.
  • The odom origin stays where the estimator starts: the front axle's position at reset. base_footprint therefore starts one wheelbase behind the origin rather than at it.
  • The stock diff-drive fallback config estimates the front axle, so it labels its odometry front_axle and publishes no TF.

docs.title: The Jetson Nano runs two Humble containers: an L4T camera container and a stock stack container
docs.text:
The Nano is limited to L4T r32 (Ubuntu 18.04). The only Humble images that keep Jetson's hardware (GStreamer nvjpegdec/nvv4l2decoder, CUDA, TensorRT) are dusty-nv's dustynv/ros:humble-*-l4t-r32.7.1. They build ROS from source with gcc-8 and Python 3.6, and apt install ros-humble-* does not work in them. The official ros:humble (22.04) arm64 image has every binary package but no access to Jetson hardware. We use both:

  • Camera container (dustynv L4T): owns the OAK and its hardware-accelerated decoding, and the CSI camera (jetson_camera), which needs Jetson Argus. Only this container builds depthai from source.
  • Stack container (official ros:humble): ros2_control, the controllers, the driver, teleop, GNSS, localisation, navigation, foxglove_bridge, and recording, all from apt.

Both use CycloneDDS (RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_cyclonedds_cpp) with --network=host --ipc=host.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Everything in the dustynv container: rejected. ros2_control, Nav2, and rtabmap would all need source builds on gcc-8 and Python 3.6, and nav2 and rtabmap have no confirmed working build there.
  • Everything in the official image: rejected. It loses the hardware decoding the camera driver depends on to stay fast.

docs.title: Transition
docs.text: The camera container stays on the existing, proven Foxy image (pilsbot/foxy-jetson, L4T, CycloneDDS) while the stack container moves to Humble. Foxy and Humble interoperate over DDS for the camera's message types. A Humble desktop on FastDDS received the Foxy camera streams at full rate (2026-11-26, see ADR 0004). Moving the camera container to the dustynv Humble image is a separate, later step and does not block the Humble port of the rest of the stack.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Full-resolution decoded frames are expensive to send between processes. Consumers of them should live in the camera container, ideally in the same process, unless measurements show the DDS copy is acceptable.
  • Open: rtabmap is meant to use the OAK's full widescreen colour resolution, and it may benefit from CUDA. Both point towards running it in the camera container, which would need a source build there. To be decided with measurements in M3/M4.
  • The Foxy line uses the same repos-file and devcontainer layout with the existing pilsbot/foxy-jetson image. The old foxy-jetson workspace branch, with its untracked gitlinks, is retired.

docs.title: We keep our own OAK camera node instead of depthai_ros_driver
docs.text: pilsbot_depthai keeps its own nodes (rgb_stereo_node, h265_node, mjpeg_node) and does not move to upstream depthai_ros_driver. The OAK encodes colour (1080p, ISP-scaled to 1280×720) and the mono pair as MJPEG on the camera. On the Nano these are decoded by a GStreamer pipeline (appsrc → [jpegparse] → nvjpegdec | nvv4l2decoder → nvvidconv → appsink), with software jpegdec/videoconvert as the fallback. Moving uncompressed frames over USB and handling them on the Nano's CPU cost too much. Getting hardware decoding to work took substantial effort, and upstream has no equivalent for the Nano.

docs.title: Verified state (2026-11-26, Nano on L4T R32.7.2, Foxy container)
docs.text:
Run as ros2 launch pilsbot_depthai mjpeg_node.launch.py nvdecoder:=nvv4l2decoder enable_raw_decode:=true from feature/h265-encoded-transport @ adc8a64:

  • nvv4l2decoder (not nvjpegdec) is the decoder in use. The NVIDIA GStreamer elements are provided by --runtime=nvidia; copying jetson_multimedia_api into the image is not needed.
  • Colour 1280×720 MJPEG at 30 fps (about 3.3 MB/s), each mono stream 400p at 15 fps (about 0.39 MB/s), decoded colour Image at about 27 fps.
  • The node uses about a third of one CPU core while idle, rising to about half a core with a subscriber on the decoded image. The rest of the Nano stays about 85% idle.
  • A Humble desktop (FastDDS, Wi-Fi) receives the streams from the Foxy/CycloneDDS container at full rate.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Only one process can open the OAK. Depth, encoders, and any on-camera neural network must share this node's pipeline.
  • nvjpegdec cannot share a process with code that uses the system libjpeg, which includes OpenCV's image decoding (see commit f40023b). Whether this also applies to the nvv4l2decoder path in use has not been checked, so composing OpenCV-heavy consumers into the decoder's process stays an open question.
  • The GStreamer pipeline is known to be brittle. Its build and runtime dependencies must be scripted in the camera container's Dockerfile, not just remembered.
  • The foxy-devel → foxy/humble branches must absorb feature/h265-encoded-transport, and all nodes must move to the Humble-era depthai-core API (CameraBoardSocket::CAM_A/B/C).

docs.title: Sidewalk segmentation runs on the OAK's neural accelerator first
docs.text: The segmentation network for the drivability map runs on the OAK-D Lite's Myriad X, inside the camera node's pipeline. This leaves the Nano's CPU and GPU free for SLAM and control. TensorRT on the Nano, in the camera container, is the fallback if the Myriad X proves too slow or the model needs unsupported layers. Picking the model is still open.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Models are limited to what OpenVINO can compile to a Myriad X blob (FP16, restricted op set), so they will be small mobile-sized networks.
  • Training images extracted from Kohlfahrt logs must be preprocessed exactly as the camera preprocesses the network's input. Recorded frames are MJPEG-compressed, while the on-camera network sees uncompressed ISP frames.

docs.title: Prefer ROS 2 standards that outlive Humble over custom equivalents
docs.text:
Where Humble offers a standard mechanism that persists in later distros, Pilsbot adopts it, even when this changes our own topics or recorded data. Custom code that only re-implements such a mechanism is removed, not ported.

First application: the custom pilsbot_sensor_broadcaster is removed. The upstream joint_state_broadcaster publishes the hoverboard and Head MCU <sensor> state interfaces on /dynamic_joint_states (control_msgs/DynamicJointState, verified with Humble 2.54 and mock hardware on 2026-11-26).

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text: • Port the custom broadcaster and keep /hoverboard_api and /head_mcu: rejected. It would keep a whole controller to maintain on every distro only to preserve topic names.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• New recordings contain /dynamic_joint_states instead of /hoverboard_api (pilsbot_driver_msgs/HoverboardAPISensors) and /head_mcu (pilsbot_driver_msgs/SteeringAxleSensorsStamped).
  • The legacy-log converter (ADR 0002) also maps those two legacy topics to /dynamic_joint_states, so datasets see one format across old and new logs.
  • The steering calibration script also reads the Head MCU values from /dynamic_joint_states, so it works while the ros2_control driver owns the Head MCU. The standalone head_mcu_node keeps publishing /head_mcu for calibration without the driver.

docs.title: Pilsbot ROS2 Workspace
docs.text:
This repository contains a preconfigured workspace for development of the Pilsbot platform. The branch humble is the primary development line. The branch foxy is the maintained legacy line, which receives backports of substantial improvements (see docs/adr).

One branch serves every target. The targets differ only in which repos files they import and which devcontainer they use:

Target Devcontainer Repos files Desktop development and simulation .devcontainer/desktop src/ros2.repos, src/desktop.repos (default) Jetson Nano, everything except the camera .devcontainer/jetson-stack src/ros2.repos Jetson Nano, OAK camera with hardware decoding .devcontainer/jetson-camera src/jetson-camera.repos

The Nano runs two containers side by side; see ADR 0003. Project vocabulary lives in GLOSSARY.md.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
You should already have Docker and VSCode with the remote containers plugin installed on your system.

  • docker
  • vscode
  • vscode dev containers extension

docs.title: Open it in vscode
docs.text:
Clone the repository to a folder of your choice with

git clone https://github.com/pilsbot/pilsbot_vscode_ws.git

or via ssh

git clone git@github.com:pilsbot/pilsbot_vscode_ws.git

Now that you've cloned your repo onto your computer, you can open it in VSCode (File->Open Folder).

When you open it for the first time, you should see a little popup that asks you if you would like to open it in a container. Say yes!

If you don't see the pop-up, click on the little green square in the bottom left corner, which should bring up the container dialog

In the dialog, select "Dev Containers: Reopen in Container" and pick the configuration for your target

VSCode will build the dockerfile inside of .devcontainer for you. If you open a terminal inside VSCode (Terminal->New Terminal), you should see that your username has been changed to ros, and the bottom left green corner should say "Dev Container"

docs.title: Setup the workspace
docs.text:
1. Import the sources and install their dependencies with ./setup.sh (desktop default), or pass the repos files for your target, e.g. ./setup.sh src/ros2.repos. The tasks Terminal->Run Task..->setup and import from workspace file do the same.
  2. Run the build task with Ctrl+Shift+B, or ./build.sh. Set BUILD_TYPE to override the default RelWithDebInfo.

docs.title: Launch the simulation
docs.text:
To test a successfull configuarion and build of the workspace you can start the Pilsbot simulation. You have two options to do so.

  1. Open a terminal in your workspace and type: ros2 launch pilsbot_simulation pilsbot.launch.py
  2. Press Ctrl+Shift+P search for ROS: Run a ROS launch file (roslaunch), type the package name pilsbot_simulation, choose a launch file e.g. pilsbot.launch.py and press Enter again to skip defining additional launch arguments.

Congratulations, you now have a setup workspace to develop on the Pilsbot platform! 🎉

If any issues occur during the setup process, do not hesitate to open an issue, so we can fix the problem as soon as possible.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text: • all packages added to the workspace should use https. If you have a Github account logged in your VSCode installation, you can easily push without the need for password authentication. You will be asked to acknowledge your login once via your browser and you're good to go.

docs.title: Pilsbot
docs.text: Pilsbot is a hobby sidewalk robot on a hoverboard drivetrain with a passively steered front axle. This glossary covers the whole workspace, including the robot, its software lines, and its recorded data.

docs.title: Vehicle
docs.text:
Front axle: The steerable axle that carries the two driven hoverboard wheels and pivots relative to the chassis. Avoid: steering axle (when meaning the whole axle), drive axle

Rear axle: The rigid, unpowered axle fixed to the chassis.

Rear axle centre: The midpoint of the rear axle, which is the robot's reference point for pose, odometry, and planning. Avoid: base (unqualified), robot origin

Wheelbase: The distance from the front axle's pivot to the rear axle centre.

Steering angle: The angle between the front axle and the chassis, measured at the pivot. Avoid: steering position, pot value (for the calibrated angle)

Passive steering: Turning the front axle by driving its two wheels at different speeds, since no motor acts on the pivot.

Acker-diff steering: Pilsbot's drive scheme, which accepts Ackermann commands (speed and steering angle) and realises them through passive steering. Avoid: diff drive, Ackermann drive (alone)

Endstop: A switch marking the mechanical limit of the steering angle on either side.

Hoverboard: The repurposed hoverboard controller board and its two hub-motor wheels, which together drive the front axle.

Head MCU: The microcontroller on the front axle that reads the steering potentiometer and the endstops.

Robot profile: The single description of one physical Pilsbot: geometry, steering calibration, device ports, and joystick mapping. Avoid: config, robot yaml

StVO lighting: Headlight, turn signal, brake, and hazard behaviour that follows German road traffic rules (StVO). Avoid: indicators (for the whole set), LEDs

docs.title: Perception
docs.text:
OAK: The OAK-D Lite camera, which provides colour, stereo depth, and on-camera neural inference. Avoid: depthai (for the device), Luxonis camera

Drivability map: A robot-local map that labels the ground ahead as drivable sidewalk, road, or not drivable. Avoid: costmap (for the semantic layer), segmentation map

docs.title: Software lines
docs.text:
Humble line: The primary development line of all Pilsbot repositories, targeting ROS 2 Humble.

Foxy line: The maintained legacy line targeting ROS 2 Foxy, which receives backports of substantial distro-independent improvements. Avoid: old branch, foxy-devel

Camera container: The Nano container with Jetson L4T libraries that owns the OAK and its hardware-accelerated decoding.

Stack container: The Nano container that runs everything else from Humble binary packages.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
Kohlfahrt log: A bag recorded during a real outing with the robot, used as raw material for datasets.

Legacy log: A bag recorded before the robot reference point moved to the rear axle centre, which must be translated before it is used with current frames.
